newsitem.title: FRANCE: Aero-engine firms see more exclusive sale pacts.
newsitem.headline: Aero-engine firms see more exclusive sale pacts.

text.p: Two major aero-engine makers said on Monday that sole supplier agreements with aircraft manufacturers will become increasingly common in the future, despite a controversy raging over exclusive deals between airliner manufacturers and airlines.
"The future will probably see more single-single agreements," Gerard Laviec, president and chief executive officer of CFM International (CFMI) told a news conference.
CFMI is a Franco-U.S. joint venture between General Electric Co and France's state-owned Snecma.
CFMI is already the sole engine supplier on the Boeing 737, the workhorse from the Boeing stable, which has outsold any other modern aircraft type.

But Europe's Airbus Industrie has used the Paris air show to attack its arch-rival Boeing over the U.S. firm's recent sole supplier agreements with Continental, Delta Air Lines and AMR Corp's American Airlines.
Airlines like to be able to shop around for engines to power their new aircraft.

But the high cost of developing new engines is forcing manufacturers to sign up exclusive deals with the airframe companies on specific aircraft types in order to recoup their investment, engine company executives said.

It was announced on Sunday that British firm Rolls-Royce Plc has been chosen to power the new Airbus A340-500 and A340-600 airliners. In announcing the deal Airbus and Rolls studiously avoided using the word exclusive, saying other engine firms could become suppliers in the longer term.

But Rolls said it was a privileged partnership which would share both the risks and rewards. "What it means is it will be a while before anyone else is around on this airplane," chairman Sir Ralph Robins told reporters.

Karl Krapek, president of rival U.S. engine maker Pratt & Whitney, a unit of United Technologies Corp, said P&W refused to equip the A340-500 and A340-600 because it could not be the exclusive supplier.

Based on P&W's estimates for potential sales of 500 of the A340 derivatives, the U.S. company would not have seen a return on the $1.5 billion investment needed for a new engine for a decade, even on an sole supplier basis, Krapek told reporters.

And even after 20 years, "the return to shareholders would have been below double digits," he said. P&W is looking for a return to shareholders of around 11 percent, while rival General Electric aims for 18 percent, he added.

The pay back for P&W would have been 23 years, if engine prices were not discounted, he said. But it would have had to pay development costs, share costs of certification, subsidise prices for the first 100 planes and take part in finance and buying back A340s.
"We expect exclusive deals to be more common for those companies looking for an return to shareholders in double digits," he said.
